stem: A 65-year-old woman has had knee and finger pain for years, worse after walking or gardening. She has bony nodules at the distal and proximal finger joints. The knee is cool without effusion, and aspirated fluid is clear and viscous with 800 WBC/µL.
oneliner: 65F + years of knee and finger pain worse with use + bony nodules at finger joints + cool knee + clear joint fluid with 800 WBC/µL → x-ray?
ask: Which x-ray finding is most likely in her knee?

options.A: Periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions across the joint
options.B: Punched-out erosions with overhanging bony edges beside the joint
options.C: Uneven joint-space narrowing with osteophytes and sclerosis
options.D: Linear calcification within the menisci and articular cartilage
options.E: Fragmented, destroyed joint with loose bone debris

whyNot.A: **Rheumatoid arthritis** pattern: needs warm swollen joints and inflammatory fluid, which she lacks
whyNot.B: **Gout** pattern: acute hot attacks with urate crystals, not years of pain worse with use and a cool knee
whyNot.D: **Chondrocalcinosis** of CPPD goes with rhomboid crystals; her bony DIP and PIP nodules point to wear
whyNot.E: **Neuropathic (Charcot) joint** needs loss of pain sensation, and her knee hurts with use

answer: Asymmetric joint-space narrowing with osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
why: Pain worse with use, **bony nodules** and **noninflammatory fluid** (WBC under 2,000/µL) mean **osteoarthritis**. Cartilage wears unevenly, so the space narrows asymmetrically, and the bone reacts with **osteophytes, sclerosis and subchondral cysts**. Erosions and osteopenia belong to inflammatory disease.

idea.rule: Osteoarthritis x-ray = narrowing + osteophytes + sclerosis + cysts; no erosions, no osteopenia.
also: Heberden nodes = DIP osteophytes
Bouchard nodes = PIP osteophytes
Joint fluid is clear, WBC under 2,000/µL
Rheumatoid arthritis instead shows periarticular osteopenia and erosions
Typical joints: knees, hips, DIP and PIP; MCP and wrist spared

stem: A 9-year-old boy still has most of his baby teeth, and a dental film shows extra unerupted teeth. His head is large with a wide forehead, and the soft spot is still palpable. His father has a similar appearance.
oneliner: 9M + retained baby teeth + extra unerupted teeth + large head + open fontanelle + father similar → exam?
ask: Which exam finding is most likely?

options.A: Shoulders that touch in front of the chest
options.B: Blue-grey sclerae with a history of fractures
options.C: Short upper arms and thighs with a long trunk
options.D: Joint hypermobility with upward lens dislocation
options.E: Several flat light-brown skin patches with smooth borders

whyNot.B: **Osteogenesis imperfecta** feature: needs fragility fractures, not extra teeth with open fontanelles
whyNot.C: **Achondroplasia** feature: rhizomelic shortening with a normal trunk, not delayed tooth eruption
whyNot.D: **Marfan** feature: lens dislocation with joint laxity, no dental or fontanelle defect
whyNot.E: **Neurofibromatosis** feature: skin patches, unrelated to supernumerary teeth and large head

answer: Shoulders brought together in front of the chest (clavicular hypoplasia)
why: Delayed closure of fontanelles with **supernumerary unerupted teeth**, dominant in families, is **cleidocranial dysplasia** from **RUNX2** loss, which impairs intramembranous ossification. The clavicles are hypoplastic or absent, so the shoulders can be **brought together in front**.

idea.rule: Cleidocranial dysplasia = RUNX2 defect: membranous bones (clavicle, skull) fail, teeth erupt late.
also: Wormian bones and open fontanelles
Hypertelorism and a wide brow
Autosomal dominant inheritance
Low serum ALP (osteoblast defect)
Clavicle and skull are the bones that fail most

stem: A 62-year-old woman has had progressive knee and hand pain for years. She has bony nodules at the distal finger joints, the joints feel cool, and aspirated fluid is clear.
oneliner: 62F + progressive knee and hand pain + DIP nodules + cool joints + clear fluid → symptom pattern?
ask: Which symptom pattern is most likely?

options.A: Morning stiffness over an hour that eases with movement
options.B: Pain that improves with activity and worsens at rest
options.C: Night pain that wakes her from sleep even when still
options.D: Symmetric swelling of the knuckles and both wrists
options.E: Stiffness lasting under 30 minutes after waking

whyNot.A: **Rheumatoid arthritis** pattern: prolonged stiffness needs warm, inflamed joints, and hers are cool
whyNot.B: Pain that **improves with use** is the inflammatory pattern; her joints are **cool** with clear fluid
whyNot.C: **Night pain at rest** raises infection, tumour or fracture; nothing in her stem points there
whyNot.D: **Symmetric MCP and wrist swelling** is rheumatoid; her nodules are at the **DIP** joints

answer: Brief morning stiffness (under 30 minutes) with pain worse after use
why: **Noninflammatory** joint fluid and **DIP nodules** point to **osteoarthritis**. Mechanical wear hurts with use and eases with rest, and **morning stiffness lasts under 30 minutes**, unlike the hour-plus stiffness of rheumatoid arthritis.

idea.rule: Mechanical joint pain worsens with use; inflammatory joint pain eases with use and gives long morning stiffness.
also: Osteoarthritis: stiffness under 30 minutes
Rheumatoid arthritis: stiffness over 1 hour
Ankylosing spondylitis: back stiffness improves with exercise
Gout: sudden hot joint, not gradual
DIP/PIP in OA; MCP/wrist in RA

stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has never used hormone therapy. She felt a sudden sharp low back pain while carrying groceries. There is midline spinal tenderness, and leg strength, sensation and reflexes are normal.
oneliner: 68F + postmenopausal, no HRT + sudden midline back pain lifting groceries + spinal tenderness + no neurologic deficit → x-ray?
ask: Which x-ray finding is most likely?

options.A: Posterior protrusion of the L5-S1 disc into the canal
options.B: Wedge-shaped loss of height of one vertebral body
options.C: Forward slip of one vertebra with a facet dislocation
options.D: Fracture line through the transverse process of L3
options.E: Narrowing of the spinal canal by thickened ligaments

whyNot.A: **Herniated disc** gives radiating leg pain with root signs; her neurologic exam is normal
whyNot.C: **Facet dislocation** needs major trauma, not lifting groceries
whyNot.D: **Transverse process fracture** follows a direct blow, and gives lateral muscle pain, not midline tenderness
whyNot.E: **Spinal stenosis** causes leg symptoms on walking, not a sudden onset

answer: Wedge or compression deformity with reduced vertebral height
why: Low-energy pain in a **postmenopausal woman** with **midline tenderness** and no deficit is a **vertebral compression fracture**. Trabecular bone is lost first, so the weak vertebral body **collapses anteriorly** and loses height.

idea.rule: Osteoporotic fractures hit trabecular bone: vertebrae, distal radius, femoral neck.
also: Colles fracture after a fall on a hand
Femoral neck fracture after a minor fall
Progressive kyphosis and height loss
Normal calcium, phosphate and ALP in osteoporosis
Estrogen loss raises osteoclast activity

stem: A 13-year-old obese boy has limped for 3 weeks and reports vague pain in his right knee. The knee examination is normal.
oneliner: 13M + obese + 3 weeks of limp + knee pain + normal knee exam → exam finding?
ask: Which examination finding is most likely?

options.A: Limited external rotation with free internal rotation
options.B: Tenderness over the tibial tubercle on palpation
options.E: Laxity of the tibia forward on the femur

whyNot.A: Free internal rotation is the opposite of this disease; the hip tends to **rotate outward**
whyNot.B: **Osgood-Schlatter** causes tibial tubercle pain, but his **knee is normal**
whyNot.C: **Trochanteric bursitis** gives point tenderness in adults and does not cause a limp with referred knee pain
whyNot.E: **Anterior drawer** tests the ACL, and his knee exam is normal

answer: Limited, painful hip internal rotation and abduction
why: An **obese adolescent** with a limp and **referred knee pain** has a **slipped capital femoral epiphysis**. The femoral head slips posteriorly and inferiorly off the neck through the physis, so **internal rotation and abduction are limited** and the hip rolls outward on flexion.

idea.rule: Adolescent limp with knee pain: examine the hip first (hip pain refers via the obturator nerve).
also: SCFE: obesity, ages 10 to 16
Legg-Calve-Perthes: age 4 to 8, avascular necrosis
Septic arthritis: fever and refuses to bear weight
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion
Fracture through the growth plate (Salter-Harris I pattern)

stem: A 55-year-old man is woken at night by an exquisitely painful, hot, red, swollen joint. The evening before, he drank heavily and ate a large meal of organ meats. Serum urate is 9.8 mg/dL, and aspirated fluid contains needle-shaped crystals.
oneliner: 55M + woken at night + hot red swollen joint + after heavy drinking and organ meats + urate 9.8 + needle crystals → joint?
ask: Which joint is most likely involved?

whyNot.A: The **knee** can be hit in gout, but less often than the big toe; it is the classic pseudogout joint
whyNot.C: The **ankle** can be involved in later attacks, but is not the typical first site
whyNot.D: The **wrist** is a late site in gout and a common site in rheumatoid arthritis
whyNot.E: The **DIP** joint points to osteoarthritis or psoriatic arthritis

why: Needle-shaped crystals and **hyperuricemia** mean **gout**. The **first MTP joint** is hit most often, because urate crystallises in cooler, distal joints and a big toe takes repeated load. Under polarised light, crystals show **negative birefringence**.

idea.rule: Acute gout loves the coolest, most loaded joints: great toe first.
also: Podagra = first MTP attack
Needle crystals, negative birefringence (yellow when parallel)
Triggers: alcohol, purines, diuretics, tumour lysis
Tophi on ears, elbows, Achilles tendon
Pseudogout: knee, rhomboid positive-birefringent crystals

stem: A 70-year-old man has aching bone pain, hearing loss and a hat size that has grown over the past years. His right femur is bowed. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised with a normal GGT, and calcium and phosphate are normal.
oneliner: 70M + bone pain + hat size increasing + hearing loss + ALP markedly raised + normal Ca and phosphate → imaging?
ask: Which imaging finding is most likely?

options.A: Diffuse loss of bone density with a very thin cortex
options.B: Fused sacroiliac joints with a bamboo-like spine
options.C: Looser zones across the pelvis and femoral necks
options.D: Thick cortex with coarse sclerotic bone
options.E: Punched-out lytic lesions scattered through the skull

whyNot.A: **Osteoporosis** has thin cortex but a normal ALP and no bowing or hearing loss
whyNot.B: **Ankylosing spondylitis** fuses the spine and sacroiliac joints; it does not enlarge the skull or bow a femur
whyNot.C: **Osteomalacia** shows Looser zones, with low calcium or phosphate and often raised ALP; his are normal
whyNot.E: **Multiple myeloma** gives lytic skull lesions, usually with high calcium and normal ALP; his calcium is normal

answer: Thickened cortex with enlarged, coarse, sclerotic bone (picture-frame vertebra)
why: A **high isolated ALP** with normal calcium and phosphate, **skull growth**, deafness and a **bowed femur** is **Paget disease of bone**. Chaotic osteoclast then osteoblast activity builds **thick, coarse, sclerotic bone**, with a **picture-frame vertebra** and increased uptake on bone scan.

idea.rule: Paget = disordered remodeling: big, dense, weak bone with a high ALP and normal Ca/Pi.
also: Hearing loss from skull foramen narrowing
High-output heart failure from vascular shunts
Osteosarcoma as late complication
Bisphosphonates reduce osteoclast activity
Urine hydroxyproline raised

stem: A 20-year-old man wakes with flaccid weakness of the legs after a large pasta dinner the night before. Similar episodes recur every few months and last hours. He is normal between episodes, and his father had similar attacks.
oneliner: 20M + recurrent flaccid weakness after carbohydrate meals + normal between episodes + father affected → lab during attack?
ask: Which laboratory value is most likely during an attack?

whyNot.B: **Hyperkalemic** periodic paralysis is triggered by potassium intake or rest after exercise, not a carbohydrate meal
whyNot.C: A **very high CK** suggests rhabdomyolysis or myopathy, and episodes here resolve completely
whyNot.D: **Hypocalcemia** gives tetany and paresthesias, not flaccid paralysis
whyNot.E: **Hypermagnesemia** needs a magnesium source such as an infusion, and would not recur after meals

why: Carbohydrate meals raise **insulin**, which drives potassium into cells, and a defect in a muscle **calcium channel** (CACNA1S) makes the fibre paralyse. **Serum potassium falls during the attack** and is normal between attacks.

idea.rule: Periodic paralysis = channelopathy; weakness tracks a potassium shift into or out of muscle.
also: Hypokalemic type: carbohydrate load or rest after exercise
Hyperkalemic type: SCN4A sodium channel, potassium triggers
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis: Asian men, with hyperthyroidism
Treatment of an attack: oral potassium
Autosomal dominant

stem: A 42-year-old man fell from a ladder and broke his arm. When the cast comes off, his wrist hangs flexed and he cannot straighten his fingers or thumb. The skin over the dorsal first web space is numb, and he can still extend his elbow.
oneliner: 42M + fall + arm fracture, cast removed + wrist drop + dorsal first web space numb + elbow extension intact → site?
ask: Which fracture site best explains these findings?

options.D: Distal radius just above the wrist

whyNot.A: **Surgical neck** injures the axillary nerve: weak shoulder abduction and lateral shoulder numbness
whyNot.B: **Medial epicondyle** injures the ulnar nerve, causing a claw hand and little-finger numbness
whyNot.D: **Distal radius** fracture lies below the wrist extensor branches; it can compress the median nerve, not cause wrist drop
whyNot.E: **Olecranon** fracture would weaken elbow extension, which he has

answer: Fracture of the humeral shaft (radial groove) injuring the radial nerve
why: **Wrist drop** with loss of finger extension and **dorsal hand numbness** is a **radial nerve** palsy. The nerve winds in the **radial groove** on the humeral shaft, and the **triceps is spared** because its branches leave higher up.

idea.rule: Match the injured nerve to the bone it hugs: radial nerve with the humeral shaft.
also: Surgical neck: axillary nerve
Medial epicondyle: ulnar nerve
Supracondylar humerus: median (anterior interosseous) nerve
Saturday night palsy: radial nerve from compression
Hip dislocation: sciatic nerve

stem: A 30-year-old woman has arm heaviness and tingling when she paints ceilings, relieved when she lowers her arm. A chest film shows an extra rib at C7.
oneliner: 30F + arm heaviness and tingling on overhead work + cervical rib on x-ray → neuro finding?
ask: Which neurologic finding is most likely?

options.A: Weak shoulder abduction with lateral arm numbness
options.B: Wrist drop with dorsal hand numbness over the thumb
options.C: Weak elbow flexion with lateral forearm numbness
options.D: Medial scapular border lifting off the chest wall
options.E: Intrinsic hand wasting with medial hand numbness

whyNot.A: **Upper trunk (C5-C6)** injury would weaken shoulder abduction; the cervical rib hits the **lower trunk**
whyNot.B: **Radial nerve** palsy gives wrist drop; this is not a lower plexus problem
whyNot.C: **Musculocutaneous** lesion weakens elbow flexion with lateral forearm numbness
whyNot.D: **Long thoracic nerve** injury gives a winged scapula, with no hand findings

answer: Wasting of intrinsic hand muscles with tingling over the medial hand and forearm
why: A **cervical rib** squeezes the **lower trunk (C8-T1)** of the brachial plexus. This causes **intrinsic hand muscle weakness** and numbness of the **medial hand and forearm**, worse with the arm raised. The subclavian vessels can also be compressed.

idea.rule: Lower trunk C8-T1 supplies the hand intrinsics and the medial arm skin; a cervical rib hits it.
also: Klumpke palsy: same roots, from traction on a raised arm
Pancoast tumour: lower trunk and Horner syndrome
Subclavian artery compression: reduced pulse on raising the arm
Subclavian vein compression: arm swelling
Erb palsy: C5-C6, waiter's tip

stem: A 50-year-old man who works as a house painter has lateral shoulder pain that builds when he works overhead. He has tenderness just below the acromion and a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction.
oneliner: 50M + painter + lateral shoulder pain overhead + painful arc + tender below acromion → maneuver?
ask: Which examination finding is most likely?

options.A: Weak abduction at 90 degrees, thumb down
options.B: Weak external rotation with the elbow at the side
options.C: Unable to lift the hand away from the lower back
options.D: Weak external rotation with the arm raised to 90 degrees
options.E: A bulge of the upper arm when the elbow is flexed

whyNot.B: **Infraspinatus** tests by external rotation at the side; his pain arc is on **abduction**
whyNot.C: **Subscapularis** is tested by the lift-off test, with the hand behind the back
whyNot.D: **Teres minor** tests by external rotation in abduction; his problem is **starting to lift** the arm, not rotating it
whyNot.E: A **Popeye bulge** follows rupture of the long head of the biceps

answer: Pain and weakness on resisted abduction with thumb down (empty can): supraspinatus
why: Overhead use with a **painful arc** points to **rotator cuff** disease, and the muscle most often torn is the **supraspinatus**. It starts abduction and holds the humeral head, so **resisted abduction with the thumb down (empty can)** is painful and weak.

idea.rule: Name the muscle by the movement that fails: initiate abduction = supraspinatus.
also: Infraspinatus: external rotation, elbow at side
Teres minor: external rotation in abduction
Subscapularis: internal rotation, lift-off test
SITS muscles make up the rotator cuff
Supraspinatus: suprascapular nerve

stem: A 70-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls on her outstretched hand. Her wrist is swollen and deformed, with tenderness over the distal radius.
oneliner: 70F + fall on outstretched hand + deformed wrist + osteoporosis → displacement?
ask: Which displacement is most likely on the lateral x-ray?

options.A: Volar shift of the distal radial fragment
options.B: Dorsal dislocation of the carpus around the lunate
options.C: Volar dislocation of the lunate from the radius
options.D: Dorsal shift of the distal radial fragment
options.E: Displaced fracture through the scaphoid waist

whyNot.A: **Smith fracture** shifts volarly and follows a fall onto the back of the flexed wrist, not the outstretched palm
whyNot.B: **Perilunate dislocation** needs high-energy trauma and centres on the carpus, not the distal radius
whyNot.C: **Lunate dislocation** needs high-energy trauma; her tenderness is over the **distal radius**
whyNot.E: **Scaphoid fracture** gives snuffbox tenderness, mostly in young adults; her tenderness is over the **distal radius**

answer: Dorsal displacement of the distal fragment (Colles, dinner-fork deformity)
why: A **fall onto the outstretched hand** in an **osteoporotic older woman** fractures the distal radius, and the fragment moves **dorsally** (Colles, **dinner-fork deformity**). A **Smith** fracture displaces volarly, after a fall on the back of the hand.

idea.rule: Fall on outstretched palm gives dorsal displacement; fall on the back of the hand gives volar.
also: Colles: dorsal, dinner-fork
Smith: volar, garden-spade
Scaphoid: snuffbox pain, risk of avascular necrosis
Osteoporosis is the main risk factor
Median nerve compression can follow

stem: A 55-year-old woman has lateral hip pain that is worse when she lies on that side. Hip movement is full and painless, and thigh sensation is normal.
oneliner: 55F + lateral hip pain + worse lying on that side + normal hip motion + intact thigh sensation → exam?
ask: Which examination finding is most likely?

options.A: Groin pain on hip internal rotation
options.D: Pain along the leg on straight-leg raising
options.E: Limited hip abduction with a shortened leg

whyNot.A: Groin pain with **internal rotation** reflects hip joint disease, but her range is **full and painless**
whyNot.C: **Anterolateral thigh numbness** is meralgia paresthetica; **sensation here is normal**
whyNot.D: **Straight-leg raise** pain reflects a lumbar root; her pain stays at the lateral hip and **sensation is normal**
whyNot.E: **Shortening with limited abduction** suggests a femoral neck fracture; her motion is full

answer: Point tenderness over the lateral greater trochanter with normal range and sensation
why: Lateral hip pain **worse lying on that side**, with **full hip motion** and normal sensation, is **trochanteric bursitis**. Pressure on the inflamed bursa over the **greater trochanter** reproduces the pain.

idea.rule: Pain you can press on the outside of the hip, with a normal joint, is a bursa or tendon, not the joint.
also: Hip joint disease: groin pain, painful internal rotation
Prepatellar bursitis: tender swelling over the kneecap, normal knee motion
Olecranon bursitis: swelling over the elbow tip, full elbow motion
Gluteal tendinopathy gives the same lateral point tenderness
Meralgia paresthetica instead causes lateral thigh numbness
